title: Why Some People Are Clutch
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article extends the sports concept of 'clutch' performance to organizational settings, defining it as the ability to stay calm, focused, and effective in high-stakes moments. Drawing on research, the author identifies several traits shared by clutch performers: high confidence rooted in preparation, a heightened ability to block out distractions, and a distinctive emotional-regulation move — converting anxiety into excitement rather than suppressing it. The piece argues the most important driver is deliberate practice under conditions that replicate real pressure, so the high-stakes moment feels familiar rather than novel. It closes by reframing clutch as an earned outcome of preparation rather than an innate trait.
points: Clutch performance isn't confined to sports — it describes any person who stays calm, focused, and delivers their best under high-stakes pressure at work.
Clutch performers tend to have high confidence in their own preparation, which gives them a sense of control rather than dread in pressure moments.
A distinguishing trait of clutch performers is converting anxiety into excitement rather than suppressing it.
The single most important driver of clutch performance is deliberately practicing under conditions that replicate real high-pressure situations.
quotes: The idea of being “clutch” refers to any person who performs exceptionally well under pressure or in high-stakes moments.
Clutch players and team members tend to have high confidence in their skills, which gives them a sense of control over unfolding situations.
Not surprisingly, clutch performers regulate their emotions in a very specific way. They channel any anxiety they feel and turn it into excitement.
They get ready for the big moments by practicing maneuvers that replicate high-pressure situations.
Clutch doesn’t reside in people. Clutch is the outcome of a highly committed performer willing to do what it takes.
